questions.q: Explain the three levels of data abstraction and the two types of data independence.
questions.model: Physical level: how data is stored. Logical level: what data is stored and relationships. View level: part of the database each user sees. Physical data independence: change storage without changing the logical schema. Logical data independence: change the logical schema without changing applications.

questions.q: Compare spanned and unspanned file organisation.
questions.model: Spanned: a record may be split across blocks; no wasted space but accessing a record can need several blocks (costly). Unspanned: a record always fits in one block; faster access but leftover space in each block is wasted. Most databases use unspanned.

questions.q: Explain two-phase locking and two limitations.
questions.model: All lock operations precede all unlocks. Growing phase: acquire locks only; lock point; shrinking phase: release only. Guarantees serializability. Limitations: reduces concurrency (holding locks unnecessarily, locking too early) and may cause deadlock (except conservative 2PL).

questions.q: Differentiate dense and sparse indexes with an example.
questions.model: Dense: an index entry for every search-key value. Sparse: entries for only some records, e.g. one per block (key 1 → B1 covering records 1-10; key 21 → B3 covering 21-30). Sparse indexes are smaller.

questions.q: List four disadvantages of file-processing systems.
questions.model: Data redundancy and inconsistency, difficulty accessing data, data isolation, integrity problems, atomicity problems, concurrent access anomalies, security problems (any four).

questions.q: C1: A file has 20,000 records of 100 B stored unspanned in 1024 B blocks, sorted on a key. Use the diagram as a guide. (a) Records per block. (b) Blocks needed. (c) A single-level sparse index has one entry per block, each entry 10 B: how many index entries and index blocks? (d) Worst-case block accesses with binary search on the file, and with the index.
questions.model: (a) floor(1024/100) = 10 records per block (24 B wasted). (b) 20,000/10 = 2,000 blocks. (c) 2,000 entries; 1024/10 = 102 entries per index block; 2000/102 = 19.6, so 20 index blocks. (d) Binary search on file: ceil(log2 2000) = 11 accesses. With the index: binary search the index ceil(log2 20) = 5, plus 1 data block = 6 accesses.

questions.q: C2: The log below is on disk when the system crashes (see the timeline diagram). <T1,start> <T1,A,100,200> <T1,B,200,400> <T1,commit> <T2,start> <T2,C,500,600>. Initial A=100, B=200, C=500. (a) Recover using deferred update. (b) Recover using immediate update. (c) Give the final values of A, B and C in each case and justify.
questions.model: (a) Deferred: T1 committed, so redo its writes: A=200, B=400. T2 has no commit, so ignore it (its write never reached the database): C=500. (b) Immediate: redo T1 using new values: A=200, B=400. T2 uncommitted, so undo using the old value: C=500. (c) Both give A=200, B=400, C=500. Deferred needs only redo; immediate needs undo for T2 and redo for T1.
